depreciation-calculator.assumptionNote: Straight-line spreads cost evenly; double-declining uses 200% of the straight-line rate and never depreciates below salvage value.

Shows the true carrying value of assets on your books.

faqs.a: For books, straight-line is simplest and most common. For tax, declining-balance (where allowed) gives bigger early deductions, which are worth more because of the time value of money. Many businesses use straight-line for reporting and an accelerated method for tax.
faqs.q: Which depreciation method should I use?

faqs.a: Your best estimate of what the asset will be worth when you retire it — resale or scrap value. Depreciation only writes off cost minus salvage, because you expect to recover the salvage amount. If you genuinely expect zero, enter 0.
No. Both methods stop at the salvage value — the schedule caps the final year's depreciation so book value lands exactly on salvage. An asset is never depreciated below what you expect to recover.
faqs.q: Can depreciation make book value negative?

faqs.a: Because money today is worth more than money later. Bigger deductions in early years cut tax bills sooner, and the time value of those savings usually beats straight-line. It also matches assets like vehicles that lose value fastest when new.

Not directly — it is a non-cash accounting charge; no money leaves when you 'depreciate'. But it reduces taxable profit, so it reduces tax paid, which does improve cash flow. That tax shield is the real financial benefit.

Use your realistic usage period, or your country's tax tables if this is for tax planning (for example 5 years for vehicles, 3 for computers in many schedules). Longer life means smaller yearly charges; be honest rather than optimistic.
faqs.q: What useful life should I enter?

depreciation-calculator.formula:
Straight-line: annual depreciation = (cost - salvage) / useful life.
Double-declining: rate = 2 / useful life; yearly depreciation = rate x book value at start of year (capped so book value never drops below salvage).
howTo: Enter the salvage (residual) value at end of life.
Set the useful life in years and pick a method.
Read the yearly schedule, book values, and total depreciation.
keyFacts: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life for accounting and tax.
Straight-line: equal depreciation every year — simple and predictable.
Double-declining-balance: 200% of the straight-line rate on the remaining book value — bigger early deductions.
Book value can never fall below salvage value under either method.
Total depreciation over the life is identical (cost minus salvage); only the timing differs.

depreciation-calculator.quickAnswer: A ₹100,000 asset with ₹10,000 salvage value over 5 years depreciates ₹18,000 a year straight-line. Double-declining-balance front-loads it: ₹40,000 in year 1, falling to ₹2,960 in year 5. Both methods depreciate exactly ₹90,000 total — they only differ in timing.
depreciation-calculator.tagline: Straight-line or declining-balance depreciation — yearly schedule and book values.
depreciation-calculator.workedExample:
Cost ₹100,000, salvage ₹10,000, life 5 years:
1. Straight-line: (100,000 - 10,000) / 5 = ₹18,000 per year; book values 82,000 → 64,000 → 46,000 → 28,000 → 10,000.
2. Double-declining, rate = 2/5 = 40%: Y1 ₹40,000 (book ₹60,000); Y2 ₹24,000 (book ₹36,000); Y3 ₹14,400 (book ₹21,600); Y4 ₹8,640 (book ₹12,960); Y5 capped at ₹2,960 (book ₹10,000).
3. Both total ₹90,000 of depreciation — timing is the only difference.

howcalc.heading: How we calculate
howcalc.s1: Straight line: (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life — the same amount every year.
howcalc.s2: Declining balance: (2 ÷ life) × remaining book value each year, never below salvage value.
